summary: Codeine is an opioid agonist relatively selective for the mu-opioid receptor, indicated for management of mild to moderate pain where an opioid is appropriate and alternatives are inadequate; it is also used as an antitussive. Analgesia is largely due to CYP2D6 conversion to morphine, so response varies with metabolizer status. It is a Schedule II controlled substance and habit forming. It carries boxed warnings for addiction/abuse/misuse, life-threatening respiratory depression, accidental ingestion, and risks with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants, plus contraindications in young children and ultrarapid metabolizers.
indications: Management of mild to moderate pain where an opioid is appropriate and alternative treatments are inadequate
Symptomatic relief of dry, non-productive cough (antitussive use)

dosage.d: 15-60 mg orally every 4 hours as needed; lowest effective dose
dosage.n: Doses above 60 mg give no added efficacy but more adverse effects; max 360 mg/24 h
Maximum 120 mg/24 h; use lowest effective dose for shortest time

dosage.d: Reduce dose and/or extend interval; start low
dosage.n: Accumulation of codeine and metabolites; monitor for sedation

dosage.d: Initiate at lower end of range and titrate slowly

admin: Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals
Assess each patient's risk of addiction, abuse and misuse before prescribing and reassess regularly
Do not co-prescribe with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants unless no alternative
Counsel patients and caregivers on safe storage, disposal, and naloxone availability
Taper gradually to avoid withdrawal after prolonged use; do not stop abruptly in dependent patients
moa: Codeine is an opioid agonist relatively selective for the mu-opioid receptor, though with much weaker affinity than morphine. Its analgesic effect is largely attributed to its CYP2D6-mediated O-demethylation to morphine, which produces analgesia by binding central and peripheral mu receptors and modulating ascending pain pathways and the perception of/response to pain. The antitussive effect is mediated by a direct action on cough centers in the medulla.

absolute: Post-operative pain management in children under 18 after tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy
Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or without resuscitative equipment
Concurrent use of MAO inhibitors or use within the last 14 days
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction including paralytic ileus
relative: Known CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers (risk of life-threatening morphine toxicity)
Elderly, debilitated, hepatic or renal impairment
monitor: Signs of misuse, abuse or addiction

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Prolonged use during pregnancy may cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognized and treated. Available data are insufficient regarding birth defect risk; animal data show fetotoxic and embryolethal effects. Use during labor may cause neonatal respiratory depression.
lact: Not recommended. Codeine and morphine are excreted in breast milk; mothers who are CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers can produce high morphine levels in milk, causing infant sedation, respiratory depression and death. If used, monitor the infant closely for sedation and feeding difficulty.
renal: Codeine and its active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment. Reduce the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval and monitor closely for sedation and respiratory depression.
hepatic: Impaired hepatic function reduces metabolism and clearance. Start at a lower dose and titrate slowly; monitor for accumulation and sedation.

major: MAO inhibitors (current or within 14 days) - serotonin syndrome, severe hypertension/CNS toxicity; contraindicated
Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants/alcohol - profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, death
CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g., fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, quinidine) - reduce conversion to morphine and analgesia
Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans) - serotonin syndrome
moderate: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., macrolides, azole antifungals) - increased codeine exposure
Mixed agonist/antagonist or partial agonist opioids - may reduce analgesia and precipitate withdrawal
Anticholinergics - increased risk of constipation, urinary retention, ileus
minor: CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine) - may lower codeine levels
interactions.food: May be taken with food to reduce gastrointestinal upset; food does not meaningfully alter efficacy.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol; combined use causes additive CNS and respiratory depression and can be fatal.
interactions.diagnostics: May increase serum amylase/lipase; can cause false-positive opioid immunoassays; reduces gut motility on imaging.

monitoring: Respiratory rate, depth and oxygen saturation, especially on initiation/dose increase
Level of sedation and pain control
Signs of opioid misuse, abuse, or addiction; consider PDMP review
counsel: Take only as directed; do not increase the dose or take more often without medical advice
Do not drink alcohol or take sedatives/sleeping tablets with codeine - it can stop your breathing
May cause drowsiness - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Use a laxative/fiber and fluids to prevent constipation
Store securely away from children and others; ask about a naloxone kit; do not breastfeed while taking it
pk: Analgesia within 30-60 minutes; antitussive effect 1-2 h
Peak plasma concentration about 1 hour after oral dosing
Store at 20-25 C in a secure, light-resistant container
pearls: Habit forming: Yes - Schedule II controlled substance with high abuse and dependence potential
BOXED WARNING: addiction/abuse/misuse, life-threatening respiratory depression, accidental ingestion fatal in children, and danger when combined with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants
Contraindicated in children under 12 and after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy in those under 18
CYP2D6 ULTRARAPID METABOLIZERS convert codeine to morphine rapidly - risk of fatal toxicity (including breastfed infants); poor metabolizers get little analgesia
Prescribe/co-dispense naloxone for patients at risk of overdose
missed: Codeine for pain is usually taken as needed - take a dose only when you have pain, not on a fixed schedule. If on a scheduled regimen, take the missed dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose; never double up.
overdose: Overdose causes respiratory depression, somnolence progressing to stupor/coma, flaccid skeletal muscles, cold clammy skin, constricted pupils, and sometimes pulmonary edema, bradycardia, hypotension and death. Secure and support the airway, give assisted ventilation and oxygen, and administer an opioid reversal agent (naloxone or nalmefene), repeating as needed since codeine outlasts a single naloxone dose. Provide supportive care for shock and pulmonary edema.
